newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Alpine skiing-Tomba could steal Kjus and Seizinger's show.
newsitem.headline: Alpine skiing-Tomba could steal Kjus and Seizinger's show.

text.p: Defending champions Lasse Kjus and Katja Seizinger are expected to dominate the upcoming Alpine skiing World Cup season but their efforts may once again be overshadowed by the comings and goings of Alberto Tomba.

Last season saw long-delayed success for both Kjus and Seizinger, whose versatile gifts had not been fully rewarded before. But for most fans, the best news of the period was the announcement that Tomba would go on skiing for another year at least.
The Italian slalom king had threatened to retire after winning in Sierra Nevada the slalom and giant world titles that had previously eluded him.
It was always widely expected that Tomba would take part in next year's world championships in Sestriere, the Italian resort where he created a ski club of which he is the sole member.
Now, the rumour has it, he may even go on until the 1998 Winter Olympics in Nagano.

But it seems that his appearances on the World Cup circuit this season will be scarce and he will probably not join the fray until the first slalom held on home snow in Madonna di Campiglio on December 17, two days before his 30th birthday.
Tomba's chances of snatching the World Cup crown he won in 1995 are therefore very slim.

Kjus, by contrast, is the undisputed favourite to retain his overall title when the season, which warmed up with two giant slaloms on the Solden glacier in Austria last month, gets underway in Park City, Utah, next weekend.

One of the rare skiers capable of winning in any of the four Alpine disciplines -- he failed only in slalom last season -- the 25-year-old Norwegian showed his ambitions and abilities were intact by winning the final downhill of the season in Lillehammer.

His only rivals for the overall title should once again be Austrian veteran Guenther Mader and fellow Norwegian Kjetil-Andre Aamodt, the 1994 World Cup winner, who is reported to be back in form after two seasons marred by injuries.
Competition looks set to be fierce for specialist World Cup titles.
Frenchmen Sebastien Amiez and Luc Alphand will be under pressure to retain their slalom and downhill crystal globes.

Tomba, Slovenia's Jure Kosir and Austrians Thomas Sykora and Mario Reiter should be Amiez' s leading rivals for the slalom honours. In giant slalom, the battle between Tomba and Swiss Michael von Gruenigen looks promising.
In downhill, the competition is wide open with Alphand, Kjus, Austrian world champion Patrick Ortlieb, Italian Kristian Ghedina and Swiss prospect Bruno Kernen among the main contenders.
For Seizinger, winning the World Cup at last after finishing four times on the podium was a real achievement.
The 24-year-old German speed specialist stands no chance in the slalom, which should again be dominated by Austrain Elfi Eder and Sweden's Pernilla Wiberg.
Seizinger has strong rivals in each of the three other events.
In giant slalom, Wiberg, Italy's Deborah Compagnoni and German Martina Ertl should provide solid opposition.
In Super-G Ertl, Italy's Isolde Kostner and Austrian Alexandra Meissnitzer look hard to beat.

In downhill, American Picabo Street has for two seasons upstaged Seizinger and she looks set to rule once more. But the new season may also see the rise of the young Swiss women's team with Sonja Nef, Marlies Oester and Karin Roten.

After men's and women's slaloms and giant slaloms in Park City, the World Cup circus stays in north America until early December. Lake Louise, Canada, sees the first women's downhill, on November 30, with Whistler hosting the opening men's downhill a week later.
